core1b.fresh_task: Two rays travel from P=(−4,0) and Q=(0,−4) toward the origin, respectively east and north. A single plane mirror through the origin allegedly sends the east-going ray north and the north-going ray east. Draw both directed rays, infer the mirror line, then decide whether a one-sided mirror can reflect both rays from the same physical face.
core1b.protected_work: Reconstruct a common reflecting-line orientation from multiple directed ray observations, then test whether a finite mirror can realize the observed paths.

stages.predict: Before solving, predict the outcome or relationship and record uncertainty.
stages.attempt: Two rays travel from P=(−4,0) and Q=(0,−4) toward the origin, respectively east and north. A single plane mirror through the origin allegedly sends the east-going ray north and the north-going ray east. Draw both directed rays, infer the mirror line, then decide whether a one-sided mirror can reflect both rays from the same physical face.
stages.reconstruct: Both heading pairs imply φ=45° mod 180°, so mirror y=x. But P lies on y−x=+4 and Q on y−x=−4, opposite sides. Thus the direction equations agree while a one-sided mirror cannot accept both incident rays. A two-sided ideal reflecting plane could.
stages.diagnose: Only if your saved response exhibits this error: Checking only equal angles without checking which side rays arrive from. Otherwise record insufficient evidence.
stages.repair: Draw vectors and reflect them; separately test signed distances from the mirror line for each incident origin.
stages.boundary_test: Can a ray with heading parallel to the mirror line be treated as an ordinary point reflection? Explain.

core1b.fresh_task: Two rays approach origin from (−3,−1) and (−3,1). A claimed vertical mirror x=0 sends their respective direction vectors (3,1),(3,−1) into (−3,1),(−3,−1). Draw both and decide whether one reflecting face suffices. What changes if the second ray instead arrives from (3,1)?
core1b.protected_work: Reconstruct a common reflecting-line orientation from multiple directed ray observations, then test whether a finite mirror can realize the observed paths.

stages.predict: Before solving, predict the outcome or relationship and record uncertainty.
stages.attempt: Two rays approach origin from (−3,−1) and (−3,1). A claimed vertical mirror x=0 sends their respective direction vectors (3,1),(3,−1) into (−3,1),(−3,−1). Draw both and decide whether one reflecting face suffices. What changes if the second ray instead arrives from (3,1)?
stages.reconstruct: Both original paths approach from x<0, and reflection negates x component while preserving y; one left-facing mirror suffices. The altered source lies at x>0, so it cannot hit the same reflecting face from its reflective side.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate two coordinate paths into directed rays and a common mirror line.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Infer common orientation, then test incident-side compatibility.
